body:
Why open technology matters

Digital services often need to exchange information with systems developed by different organisations. A public service may need to check a document, receive a payment and update an official record. If each component uses completely incompatible methods, integration becomes expensive and users may have to repeatedly submit the same information.

Open technologies can make systems easier to understand, reuse, adapt and connect. However, the word open has different meanings when applied to standards, software, data and interfaces. These concepts should not be treated as synonyms.

Four important concepts

ConceptWhat is made available?Main purposeImportant qualification
Open standardA publicly accessible technical specification available for independent implementation; India's e-governance policy requires necessary patent claims to be available royalty-free for the standard's lifetime.Enable compatible systems to communicate or exchange information.Software using the standard need not itself be open source.
Open-source softwareSource code under a licence permitting use, study, modification and redistribution.Allow inspection, adaptation and reuse of software.Licence conditions still apply; public visibility alone may be insufficient.
Open dataData made available for anyone to access, use, reuse and redistribute under an open licence.Support research, transparency, innovation and further services.Personal, confidential and sensitive data are not automatically open.
Open APIA documented application interface made accessible under stated terms.Permit approved interaction between software systems.Access restrictions may apply; the underlying source code may remain closed.

Open standards and interoperability

A standard establishes an agreed method, rule or format. An open standard helps independent developers implement compatible products without depending on one provider's undisclosed technical method.

For example, if 2 applications use a common, appropriately specified format to exchange information, they are more likely to interpret the information consistently. A standard makes interoperability possible, but actual interoperability also depends on correct implementation, compatible meaning and suitable administrative arrangements.

Open standards can reduce vendor lock-in, a situation in which replacing one supplier becomes difficult because systems depend heavily on that supplier's proprietary formats or products. They can also support long-term maintenance and competition.

What makes software open source?

Software is written using human-readable instructions called source code. Open-source software is distributed under a licence that gives users defined rights to inspect, use, change and redistribute that code.

Publicly displaying code without granting reuse and modification rights does not necessarily make the software open source. Likewise, a free-to-download application may still be proprietary.

Open-source software can be used by governments, businesses and individuals. It may be provided without a licence fee, but operating the software still requires resources for infrastructure, maintenance, training, security and support.

What is an API?

An Application Programming Interface (API) specifies how one software application can request information or a function from another. For example, a government application might use an approved API to request verification of a digitally issued document.

An API is not the same as a database. It is the defined interface through which permitted interaction occurs. An API may require authentication, authorization and other security controls. Making an API available for integration does not require exposing all underlying records to everyone.

Open data and the limits of public disclosure

Open government data generally refers to shareable, non-sensitive government data released in usable formats and under appropriate reuse conditions. Examples may include published statistical tables or public-service datasets that contain no information prohibited from disclosure.

India's National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy, 2012 (NDSAP) promotes access to shareable data generated through public funds. The Open Government Data Platform India provides a mechanism for such publication.

The Government Open Data License - India permits lawful commercial and non-commercial reuse of covered data, subject to conditions including attribution. It does not automatically cover personal information, sensitive data or information the provider has no authority to license.

India's policy approach to open technology

The Government of India's Policy on Adoption of Open Source Software promotes open-source solutions as a preferred option in relevant government information-technology systems. The Policy on Open APIs encourages suitable interfaces for integration and interoperability. These policies support reuse and reduce unnecessary fragmentation, while actual procurement and implementation remain subject to applicable requirements.

Open standard: how systems agree to communicate. Open source: rights relating to software code. Open data: permitted access and reuse of datasets. Open API: a defined interface through which applications interact.

Prelims focus

  • Open standards support compatibility between independently developed systems.
  • Open-source software requires suitable licence rights, not merely visible code.
  • An API is an application interface; it is not necessarily an open database.
  • NDSAP was approved in 2012 and concerns shareable government data.
  • The Government Open Data License - India includes attribution requirements and excludes specified sensitive information.
  • Trap: Free software, open-source software, open APIs and open data are not interchangeable concepts.

[Sources: Government of India, Policy on Adoption of Open Source Software for Government of India, 2015, objectives and policy framework; Government of India, Policy on Open Application Programming Interfaces for Government of India, policy framework listed on e-Governance Standards and Guidelines; Press Information Bureau, 'National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy – 2012 approved,' 9 February 2012; Open Government Data Platform India, 'Government Open Data License - India,' sections 3, 4 and 6; sources consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Four distinct forms of openness surround a digital service, with interoperability defined separately and a reminder that open source does not make personal data public.
pictures.caption: Open standards, source code, data and APIs address different aspects of digital systems.

title: Open Standards, Open-Source Software, Open Data and Open APIs

body:
Digital systems as shared development resources

Roads, electricity and communication networks support many different economic activities. In a comparable way, certain digital systems provide common capabilities that multiple organisations can use to deliver services. Examples include verifying an identity, transferring money or securely exchanging information.

Digital development discussions distinguish between digital public goods (DPGs) and digital public infrastructure (DPI). Their names are similar, but their meanings are not identical.

What is a digital public good?

A digital public good is a digital solution, such as open-source software, open data, an open AI system or an open content collection, that meets relevant openness, safety, privacy and development-oriented requirements. The Digital Public Goods Alliance uses a defined standard to assess solutions for formal DPG recognition.

The central idea is reusability under suitable open conditions. An eligible software solution may be adapted by different organisations and countries instead of being independently developed from the beginning each time.

The Digital Public Goods Alliance (DPGA) maintains the Digital Public Goods Standard. Its assessment framework uses 9 main indicators, covering matters such as Sustainable Development Goal relevance, open licensing, ownership, documentation, platform independence, privacy, security and standards or best practices. A solution recognized through this assessment is listed in the DPG Registry.

Not every open-source project automatically satisfies these criteria. A reusable software project may lack adequate documentation, have harmful privacy practices or fail another requirement. Similarly, not every government-operated website is automatically a recognized digital public good.

What is digital public infrastructure?

Digital public infrastructure refers to shared digital systems that support essential functions across many services and sectors, such as identity verification, payments and appropriate data exchange.

Under the framework discussed during India's G20 Presidency in 2023, DPI is described as shared, secure and interoperable digital systems that can be built on open standards and specifications and, where appropriate, open-source software. The approach emphasizes broad usability, accountability, inclusion and suitable governance.

DPI is not limited to one government department's website. Its value comes from providing a function that many public and private services can use. A payment interface used by different banks and payment applications is a clearer illustration of shared infrastructure than a single-purpose departmental information page.

Digital public goods and infrastructure compared

FeatureDigital public goodDigital public infrastructure
Core ideaOpen and reusable digital solution meeting relevant criteria.Shared digital system enabling important functions across services.
Main emphasisLicensing, reuse, adaptability and public-benefit safeguards.Interoperability, trusted operation, access and large-scale service enablement.
Typical formOpen-source identity software or openly licensed public-interest dataset.Identity, payment or trusted data-exchange infrastructure.
RelationshipMay be used to build DPI.Need not have every component recognized as a DPG.

MOSIP: an open-source identity platform

MOSIP stands for Modular Open Source Identity Platform. It is an open-source, open-standards-based foundational identity platform anchored at the International Institute of Information Technology Bangalore (IIIT-B).

MOSIP provides reusable technology that governments may adapt for identity-system functions such as enrolment, identity management and verification. It illustrates how an openly available platform can support the development of national digital identity systems.

MOSIP is not another name for Aadhaar. Aadhaar is India's national identity system operated under its own statutory framework, whereas MOSIP is a reusable identity-technology platform that different jurisdictions may adopt or adapt.

Public benefit does not automatically establish open-source status. A government portal may deliver an important public service without making all its software open source. Equally, DPI can use a combination of open and non-open components while remaining subject to governance and interoperability requirements.

Prelims focus

  • DPG means Digital Public Good; DPI means Digital Public Infrastructure.
  • The DPGA's Digital Public Goods Standard uses 9 main assessment indicators.
  • Digital identity, digital payments and trusted data exchange are key DPI functions.
  • The G20 framework for DPI was discussed under India's 2023 Presidency.
  • MOSIP stands for Modular Open Source Identity Platform and is anchored at IIIT-B.
  • Trap: DPI, DPG and an ordinary government website are not necessarily the same category.

[Sources: Digital Public Goods Alliance, 'DPG Application FAQs,' definition of a digital public good; DPGA, 'Digital Public Goods Standard,' 9 indicators and registry requirements; G20, Framework for Systems of Digital Public Infrastructure, 19 August 2023, paragraphs on shared systems and core functions; MOSIP, official documentation, 'What is MOSIP?'; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter 8, 'Infrastructure,' printed pp. 140–141; sources consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A reusable DPG such as MOSIP may help build shared digital infrastructure that supports government or private services.
pictures.caption: A reusable digital public good can support shared infrastructure used by many services.

title: Digital Public Goods and Digital Public Infrastructure: Definitions and Distinctions

body:
How shared digital capabilities support services

A government or business service may require several distinct capabilities. It may need to establish a customer's identity, receive a payment, obtain an authentic document and securely exchange information with another authorized system. Building a completely independent method for each function in every application creates duplication.

Digital public infrastructure allows services to use common capabilities subject to the rules of each system. In India, Aadhaar, Unified Payments Interface (UPI) and DigiLocker illustrate different functions within the wider digital ecosystem.

Important Indian systems and their functions

SystemPrimary functionImportant distinction
AadhaarFoundational identification and permitted identity authentication or verification.Does not itself transfer money or establish citizenship.
UPIInteroperable instant payment capability between participating bank accounts.Payment infrastructure, not an identity or citizenship document.
DigiLockerAccess, storage, sharing and verification of authentic digital documents.A digital document service, not another Aadhaar number.
API SetuSupports permitted integration and exchange between participating applications through APIs.An integration mechanism; it does not make every connected dataset public.

UPI: interoperable digital payments

UPI stands for Unified Payments Interface. It was developed by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). UPI enables instant transfers between participating bank accounts and supports payments through multiple participating applications.

The important concept is interoperability. A payer and recipient need not use the same application's interface, provided the relevant institutions and applications participate in the compatible payment system and the transaction meets applicable conditions.

A UPI ID or payment address identifies where a payment request should be directed. It is not proof of citizenship. A UPI PIN is used to authorize applicable payment transactions. Knowing a person's UPI ID does not authorize someone else to debit the person's account.

DigiLocker: trusted digital documents

DigiLocker is a Digital India initiative of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. It provides a digital document wallet through which users can access and share documents issued by participating authorized organisations.

In this ecosystem, an issuer is an authorized organisation that provides an authentic digital document, such as an educational certificate. A requester is an authorized organisation seeking permitted access to a document for verification. The existence of an issued digital document differs from a user's self-uploaded file: the former carries the authority of the issuing organisation within the applicable system.

A digital signature can help establish a document's origin and detect unauthorized alteration. However, the receiving organisation must still determine whether the document satisfies the requirements of the particular service.

Interoperability has more than one aspect

Interoperability is the ability of different systems to exchange information and use it appropriately. It involves more than merely connecting 2 computers.

  • Technical interoperability: Systems communicate using compatible interfaces, formats and methods.
  • Semantic interoperability: Systems understand the exchanged information in the same intended sense. For example, the meaning of a certificate field should remain consistent.
  • Organizational interoperability: Participating organisations have appropriate procedures, responsibilities and permissions for the exchange.

Compatible APIs may provide a technical connection, but accurate interpretation and lawful access remain necessary. Systems should not exchange personal data merely because a technical connection exists.

Example: completing an online government application

A citizen applies online for a government certificate that requires payment and supporting documents. The service may use an approved login or identity-verification method to establish who is applying. DigiLocker or another permitted route may supply a relevant issued document. A UPI payment option may allow the applicant to pay an applicable fee. APIs can support permitted exchanges between the application and relevant systems.

The issuing department still decides whether the application satisfies the rules and whether the certificate should be granted. The presence of shared infrastructure does not transfer the department's decision-making authority to UPI, DigiLocker or a login provider.

Prelims focus

  • UPI expands to Unified Payments Interface and was developed by NPCI.
  • UPI supports instant, interoperable bank-account payments.
  • A UPI PIN authorizes applicable transactions; a UPI ID is a payment address.
  • DigiLocker is a Digital India initiative associated with authentic digital documents.
  • Technical, semantic and organizational interoperability address different conditions for successful exchange.
  • Trap: A digital identity provider, a payment system and a document issuer do not perform the same function.

[Sources: National Payments Corporation of India, 'UPI Frequently Asked Questions,' UPI and UPI PIN definitions; DigiLocker, official website, 'About DigiLocker,' and 'Organizational Model,' issuers and requesters; DigiLocker, 'Security Architecture,' permitted document exchange; Government of India, e-Governance Standards and Guidelines, 'Interoperability Framework for e-Governance'; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, API Setu programme materials; sources consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: An application uses separate identity, document and payment functions; permitted APIs connect systems, while the department independently approves or rejects.
pictures.caption: Digital identity, payment and document services perform different functions in an integrated service.

title: India's Digital Public Infrastructure: Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker and Interoperability
